2.text: In funeral ceremonials gloves with only three fingers are used. They are

3.text: worn by the woman who cuts up the body, in order to keep her hands free

4.note: A small ink speck sits above the word between "cont" and "amination" — no letter or mark of the notation is missing there; ruled a printing artifact, not a diacritic.

5.text: Mittens are not made double, because the tough

6.text: reindeer-leg skin of which they are made would make it

7.text: impossible to handle anything with a double mitten. During

8.text: a journey the hands are always kept in motion sufficiently

9.text: to remain warm. The working-people of other tribes of

10.text: the country have mittens of the same shape and material.

11.text: The Russians, on the other hand, have adopted, besides

12.text: the type described above, another style of mitten, which

13.text: is made of curried skin, lined inside with soft fawn-skin,

14.text: and trimmed around the wrist with a narrow strip of fluffy

15.text: beaver-skin. A little above the wrist the mitten has a
15.note: A raised comma-shaped ink mark sits immediately after "above"; the word needs no apostrophe here ("above the wrist"), so this is ruled a printing speck, not a keyed mark.

16.text: cross-slit through which the hand may be conveniently

17.text: thrust for any special work requiring the use of the fingers.

18.text: The slit is trimmed with fluffy fur, squirrel or beaver, to

19.text: keep the cold out. These mittens are really better suited

20.text: for short walks within the village than for real work or

22.text: The Russian merchants and officials have adopted

23.text: still another style of mitten, a combination of the two above described. It is

24.text: double. The outside is made of the soft leg-skins of the white, red, or gray

25.text: fox; and the inside, of the belly-skins of the same animals. The palm and

26.text: the inner surface of the thumb are of cloth or curried leather, which makes

27.text: the mitten fairly flexible in spite of its excessive thickness. The cross-slit

28.text: above the wrist is usually present, but the mittens are so heavy that no cold

29.text: enters it. These mittens, I think, are the largest in the world. Those in

30.text: the collection are 32 cm. long and 15 cm. wide. The thumb is 8 cm. long.

31.text: The Koryak and the Kamchadal, and even the Gilyak and the Tungus of

32.text: the Amur River, have, in their turn, imitated in native material various patterns

33.text: of mittens and gloves made by the Russians. These show a mixture of native

34.text: and Russian elements. Thus the Koryak have mittens and gloves of curried

35.text: leather, lined with fur, with a cross-slit under the wrist. The Tungus of the

36.text: Amur (see specimen, Cat. No. (??/????)) have mittens of the leg-skin of the reindeer,
36.note: AMNH catalogue number set as a stacked fraction (read 70/915); deferred per keying_spec.md §2.8, keyed as the fixed literal (??/????).

37.text: with palms of curried leather and a cross-slit bordered with fur; also mittens

38.text: of curried leather lined with fur (see specimen, Cat. No. (??/????)).

39.text: The Chukchee cap (Fig. 173) fits the head closely, and its triangular

40.text: flaps snugly enclose the ears. These ends are joined by a band of cloth or

41.text: curried leather of such length that when they are crossed under the chin the

42.text: band will hold them in place by being pulled over the crown of the head
